title: Shabana Azmi Set for Rare Feat With Two Films Releasing on Independence Day
excerpt: The veteran actor stars in both Batwara 1947 and Awarapan 2, both hitting theaters on August 14 — a double release she says last happened over four decades ago.
body:
• Shabana Azmi will appear in two major Bollywood releases — Batwara 1947 and Awarapan 2 — both opening on August 14, 2026
  • In Batwara 1947, she plays a Hindu woman who refuses to leave Lahore after Partition; in Awarapan 2, she plays the primary antagonist
  • Azmi says the last time she had two films release on the same day was in 1983, over four decades ago
  • Both films arrive during the crucial Independence Day weekend, one of the biggest release windows in Indian cinema

When Indian audiences head to theaters this Independence Day weekend, they will find Shabana Azmi on both sides of the box office battle. The veteran actor stars in two of the holiday weekend's biggest releases — Sunny Deol's partition drama Batwara 1947 and Emraan Hashmi's action sequel Awarapan 2 — both opening on August 14, 2026.

It is a rare double release for any actor, and one that Azmi herself has noted carries personal significance. According to the actor, the last time she had two films release on the same day was in 1983 — more than four decades ago, during a period when she routinely shuttled between art-house and commercial cinema, sometimes shooting two films on the same day.

Two Distinct Roles

The two films could not be more different in tone and setting, and Azmi plays dramatically contrasting characters in each.

In Batwara 1947, directed by Rajkumar Santoshi and produced by Aamir Khan, Azmi plays the lone Hindu woman who refuses to leave her home in Lahore after the 1947 Partition. The film, based on Asghar Wajahat's acclaimed play Jis Lahore Nai Vekhya, O Jamya E Nai, follows an Indian Muslim family forced to migrate to Pakistan and allotted a house that already has an occupant who will not go. The film stars Sunny Deol and Preity G. Zinta, with music by A.R. Rahman and lyrics by Javed Akhtar.

"It's our fortune and luck that we get to share this release date with the legend Sunny Deol."

— Vishesh Bhatt, Producer, Awarapan 2

In Awarapan 2, produced by Vishesh Bhatt and directed by Nitin Kakkar, Azmi takes on the role of the main antagonist opposite Emraan Hashmi's Shivam Pandit. The sequel picks up nearly two decades after the events of the 2007 original, which initially underperformed at the box office but went on to develop a cult following. The sequel also stars Disha Patani and Suvinder Vicky.

A Box Office Clash With History

The August 14 clash echoes a box office rivalry from 2007, when Sunny Deol and Emraan Hashmi last went head-to-head. That year, Deol's Apne and Hashmi's original Awarapan released in the same window, with Apne emerging as the commercial winner despite Awarapan's critical acclaim.

Nearly two decades later, the dynamics have shifted. Awarapan 2 carries significant pre-release buzz, with its trailer generating strong audience reception. Batwara 1947, meanwhile, brings the weight of a star-studded ensemble, a major production house, and a story rooted in one of the subcontinent's most consequential historical events.

Azmi's Six-Decade Career

For Azmi, the double release is a testament to her enduring relevance across Bollywood's evolving landscape. A five-time National Film Award winner and recipient of the Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan, she has built a career spanning over 150 films, moving between intimate art-house dramas and large-scale commercial productions with equal command. Her recent projects include Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani and the Netflix series Dabba Cartel.

That she can anchor significant roles in two competing releases at this stage of her career speaks to both her range and the industry's continued reliance on performers who bring craft and credibility to ensemble casts.

What's at Stake

The Independence Day weekend is one of Indian cinema's most important release windows, drawing large audiences to theaters during the national holiday. For diaspora audiences in North America and the UK, both films will be available in international markets, offering a rare opportunity to see one of Indian cinema's most respected performers in two sharply different roles on the same day.
